summary: This specification describes version 2 of the Optimized Link State Routing Protocol (OLSRv2) for Mobile Ad Hoc Networks (MANETs). It lets wireless devices without fixed infrastructure share routes with one another.

eli5.summary: Many phones form a network with no towers. This is how each one helps share where everyone is so messages find a way.

subtitle: A proactive link state routing protocol for wireless ad hoc networks that uses multipoint relays to cut control traffic.

tldr.problem: Mobile ad hoc networks have no fixed infrastructure, a changing topology and lossy wireless links, so classic link state routing floods too much control traffic and cannot easily use metrics other than hop count.
tldr.mechanism: Each router picks two small sets of symmetric neighbors, flooding MPRs and routing MPRs, that cover its 2-hop neighbors. Only flooding MPRs relay control messages, and only routers chosen as routing MPRs advertise link state in TC messages, together with additive link metrics.
tldr.outcome: OLSRv2 is a Proposed Standard that succeeds OLSR (RFC 3626) while leaving that RFC in place for further experimentation. It has been updated by RFC 7183, RFC 7187, RFC 7188 and RFC 7466.

today: RFC 7181 is a Proposed Standard that has not been obsoleted, but the metadata lists RFC 7183, RFC 7187, RFC 7188 and RFC 7466 as updating it: RFC 7183, RFC 7187, RFC 7188 and RFC 7466. It does not obsolete RFC 3626, which the text says is left in place for further experimentation.

sections.title: What OLSRv2 Is For
sections.content:
The Optimized Link State Routing Protocol version 2 (OLSRv2) is the successor to OLSR version 1 (RFC 3626). It keeps the same basic mechanisms and algorithms, but adds the ability to use a link metric other than hop count when choosing shortest routes, a more flexible and efficient signaling framework, and some simplification of the messages.

It is built for Mobile Ad Hoc Networks (MANETs). It is a table-driven, proactive protocol: routers exchange topology information regularly, so routes are continuously maintained and instantly available, and data traffic suffers no route discovery delay. It suits networks with a dynamic topology where messages may be lost, for example to collisions on wireless media, and it is optimized for large and dense networks. It works in a completely distributed manner with no central entity.

OLSRv2 makes no assumptions about the link layer. It builds on the neighborhood discovery protocol NHDP (RFC 6130) and the packet and message format of RFC 5444, with optional jitter from RFC 5148. These were all originally created as part of OLSRv2 but specified separately for wider use.
sections.eli5: It is a way for devices in a changing wireless crowd to always know a path to each other, without any boss device or fixed towers.

sections.title: Multipoint Relays and the Big Picture
sections.content:
The key idea is the multipoint relay (MPR). Each router selects two sets of MPRs from its symmetric (bidirectional) 1-hop neighbors, each set covering all of its symmetric 2-hop neighbors. These are flooding MPRs, which achieve flooding reduction, and routing MPRs, which achieve topology reduction.

With MPR flooding, a router retransmits a control message only if it first received it directly from a router that selected it as a flooding MPR. With topology reduction, routers declare link state only for their routing MPR selectors, and a router that no one selected as a routing MPR need not send link state at all. Using symmetric links also avoids the problems of sending data over unidirectional links.

Two message types do the work. HELLO messages come from NHDP and are extended to carry the originator address, willingness, link metrics and MPR choices. They are never forwarded. TC (Topology Control) messages are sent periodically on all OLSRv2 interfaces and flooded across the MANET using MPR flooding. Each router keeps information bases that record what it has learned: local, interface, neighbor, topology, and received-message information.
sections.eli5: Instead of everyone repeating every message, each device picks a few helper friends that together can reach everyone nearby. Only those helpers repeat the news.

sections.title: Selecting the MPRs
sections.content:
Each router MUST select, from its willing symmetric 1-hop neighbors, a flooding MPR set and a routing MPR set. Any process may be used if it meets the stated properties, and routers can interoperate even when using different algorithms. The RFC gives an example algorithm in Appendix B.

The properties are defined on a Neighbor Graph with a set N1 of willing 1-hop neighbors and a set N2 of 2-hop neighbors. A valid MPR set contains every neighbor with willingness WILL_ALWAYS, covers every 2-hop neighbor that cannot be reached directly, and keeps the minimum distance route to each 2-hop neighbor. Keeping the sets small keeps protocol overhead low, though they need not be minimal.

The two sets differ. Flooding MPRs may or may not use metrics, and when they do they use outgoing link metrics. Routing MPRs must use metrics, specifically incoming neighbor metrics. Flooding MPRs are selected per OLSRv2 interface; routing MPRs need not be. A router MUST recalculate an MPR set whenever the current one no longer satisfies the conditions.

Willingness lets a router say how ready it is to serve. Each router has WILL_FLOODING and WILL_ROUTING between WILL_NEVER (0) and WILL_ALWAYS (15), with WILL_DEFAULT recommended as 7. Routers with generous resources, such as a permanent power supply, can take on more of the work.
sections.eli5: Each device looks at its neighbors and picks the smallest group of friends that can reach everyone two steps away. Friends who are tired can say no, and friends who love helping can say always.

sections.title: Link Metrics and Parameters
sections.content:
Link metrics in OLSRv2 are additive and directional, assessed at the receiver, and routes are those with the minimum sum of metrics. The RFC does not define what a metric means physically, and the process that determines incoming metric values is outside its scope. It warns against simply defaulting to equal metrics (hop count) without considering whether that fits.

Metrics are carried in a compressed 12-bit form made of a 4-bit exponent and an 8-bit mantissa. The constants are MINIMUM_METRIC = 1 and MAXIMUM_METRIC = 16776960, and the representable value is (257+a)2^b - 256.

Protocol parameters can be changed dynamically and need not match across routers. The RFC's proposed values include TC_INTERVAL of 5 seconds, TC_MIN_INTERVAL of one quarter of that, T_HOLD_TIME of 3 times TC_INTERVAL, and 30 seconds for the hold times that remember processed and forwarded messages. TC_HOP_LIMIT is 255, and the maximum must be at least the network diameter in hops. TC messages MUST NOT be sent purely in response to changes, because a router cannot know about distant routers joining.
sections.eli5: Each wireless hop gets a score for how good it is, and the best route is the one whose scores add up to the smallest total. Scores are squeezed into a small number to save space.

sections.title: HELLO and TC Messages
sections.content:
OLSRv2 packets use the format of RFC 5444 and MUST be sent using either the manet IP protocol number or the manet UDP port, and MAY use the link-local multicast address LL-MANET-Routers. HELLO and TC messages MUST both use IP or both use UDP in a given MANET so they can share a packet.

The specification defines two Message TLVs and four Address Block TLVs. MPR_WILLING in HELLO messages holds the two willingness values. CONT_SEQ_NUM in TC messages holds the Advertised Neighbor Sequence Number (ANSN), which lets receivers tell fresh information from old even if messages arrive out of order. LINK_METRIC carries link or neighbor metrics, MPR marks neighbors selected as MPRs, NBR_ADDR_TYPE says whether an address is an originator or routable address, and GATEWAY gives the hops to an attached network.

A TC message carries the originator address, a sequence number, a hop limit, the ANSN, a validity time, and the advertised neighbors and attached networks. TC messages can be complete, advertising all routing MPR selectors, or incomplete, reporting additions only. Router TC messages are sent every TC_INTERVAL by default, and a router with nothing left to advertise sends empty TC messages for A_HOLD_TIME to speed removal of old information. TC messages carry one IANA-assigned Message Type, value 1.
sections.eli5: HELLO is a quick wave to the neighbors next door. TC is a bulletin about who your close friends are, passed along the helper chain, with a number so people can tell which bulletin is newer.

sections.title: Flooding, Duplicates and Routes
sections.content:
A router silently discards any message it originated itself. For a TC message to be forwarded, the sending address must match a symmetric neighbor on the receiving interface, the message must not be a duplicate, and it must come from one of the router's flooding MPR selectors. Received, Processed and Forwarded sets record messages so each is processed once and forwarded at most once per interface. Sequence numbers are 16 bits and compared with wraparound in mind.

From HELLO and TC information a router builds a Network Topology Graph. A "backbone" of routers, each identified by its originator address, is extended with routable addresses and attached networks. The Routing Set MUST hold the shortest paths to all destinations from all local OLSRv2 interfaces, using any algorithm. If two paths have equal total metric, the one with fewer hops SHOULD be used. Changes to the Routing Set need no messages, and the IP routing table should be updated from it.

Attached networks are how a router acts as a gateway to non-OLSRv2 networks. The RFC recommends giving a dedicated IP prefix to the OLSRv2 routing domain and advertising it into any external domain.
sections.eli5: Each helper only repeats a note the first time it hears it and only if it came from a friend who picked it. Then every device uses the notes to draw its own map and find the cheapest path.

sections.title: Security
sections.content:
As a proactive routing protocol, OLSRv2 is a potential target for various attacks. The architecture lets deployments choose their security features, since MANET deployments range from needing near-unbreakable security to almost none. Implementations can reject messages for external reasons, such as an Integrity Check Value that cannot be verified.

A conformant implementation MUST at minimum implement the mechanisms of RFC 7183, which provide integrity and replay protection of control messages using a timestamp TLV and an ICV TLV with a SHA-256-based HMAC and manually managed shared keys. The baseline use case is short-lived deployments, for example up to a couple of months. Longer deployments should consider alternatives such as rekeying. Automated key management is not mandated.

Where OLSRv2 connects to an external routing domain, care MUST be taken not to inject insecure or untrustworthy information from it and to validate information before injecting it.
sections.eli5: Because everyone trusts the notes they get, a sneaky kid could pass fake notes. So notes get a secret stamp that only friends who know the secret can make or check.

fields.desc: Bits 0-3 indicate link or neighbor metric and incoming or outgoing.

fields.name: Exponent (b)
fields.desc: Bits 4-7 hold the exponent of the compressed metric.

fields.desc: Bits 8-15 hold the mantissa of the compressed metric.

items.label: Message TLV in HELLO
items.desc: Bits 0-3 hold WILL_FLOODING and bits 4-7 hold WILL_ROUTING.

items.desc: Carries a link or neighbor metric, 2 octets.
